[The reset]{.kicker}

## Architecture uses many evidence types

Designers draw on a wide range of inputs. None is automatically strong or weak — strength depends on the decision it served.

- precedent
- standards and code
- site observation
- stakeholder input
- simulation
- measurement
- published research
- benchmarks and case comparisons

---

## Not all inputs are equal

::: {.concept-card}
[The useful question]{.card-title}
**Did this input actually reduce uncertainty for the decision?**
:::

If it did not, it may have been something else wearing the costume of evidence:

- inspiration
- convention
- assumption
- noise

---

[The recurring engine]{.kicker}

## A fast evidence ladder

The same input can sit high or low depending on fit. As a rough first sort:

:::: {.three-step}
::: {.step-box}
[Usually stronger]{.card-title}
Measured performance · well-matched comparative evidence · relevant standards and verified constraints
:::
::: {.step-box}
[Often in between]{.card-title}
Simulation output · stakeholder input · a single relevant precedent — strong **only** if assumptions and context hold
:::
::: {.step-box}
[Usually weaker]{.card-title}
Isolated precedent images · vague "best practice" · unsupported confidence from the designer
:::
::::

::: {.warning-card}
A weak input is not forbidden — it just cannot carry a strong claim on its own.
:::

---

## A1 core move

::: {.concept-card}
[Not the goal]{.card-title}
Proving that your earlier design was right.
:::

Do this instead:

- name the decision clearly
- separate evidence from assumption
- admit what was missing
- define what you would need next time

---

## Fast audit template

For each input you actually used, name its type, its honest strength, and what it really supported.

| Input used then | Type | Strength | What it really supported |
|---|---|---|---|
| precedent image | visual precedent | low–medium | form and atmosphere, not performance |
| simulation screenshot | model output | medium | comparison only if assumptions were sound |
| code requirement | standard | high within its scope | compliance, not overall quality |

[Take-away artifact]{.kicker}

## A1 evidence audit, not notes

By the end of Week 2, your A1 board should contain a visible audit layer.

::: {.tool-panel}
::: {.zone .input}
**Input** one decision image + sources used then
:::
::: {.zone .operation}
**Sort** evidence / precedent / assumption / preference
:::
::: {.zone .output}
**Output** weak-link diagnosis and missing test
:::
::: {.zone .check}
**Quality check** the claim gets weaker or stronger when the source is removed
:::
:::

---

## Common overclaims

::: {.warning-card}
[Watch for these in your own A1]{.card-title}

- "there was evidence" when there was only precedent
- "the model proved it" when the assumptions were weak
- "users prefer this" from a tiny or biased sample
- "this is best practice" without context
:::

The strongest move is catching one of these in your **own** work before anyone else does.

---

[Anecdote · evidence that was never audited]{.kicker}

## 2010: an austerity argument built on a spreadsheet error

::: {.warning-card}
[What happened]{.card-title}
A widely cited economics paper (Reinhart & Rogoff) reported that economic growth collapses once public debt passes 90% of GDP. The claim was used to justify austerity policy in several countries. In 2013 a graduate student rechecking the workbook found an Excel formula that **left out five rows** — once corrected, the dramatic threshold largely disappeared.
:::

::: {.example-card}
[The lesson]{.card-title}
A result nobody can re-open and audit is a vibe with a number attached. Evidence is only as strong as your ability to trace how it was computed.
:::

[Uncertainty check]{.kicker}

## Polished evidence still needs inspection

::: {.uncertainty-check}
**Question for your A1**
Which piece of evidence in your old project looked convincing because it was visually polished, not because it was actually strong?
:::

If the answer is a render, precedent image, exported map, or simulation screenshot, write down what would have to be checked before it could carry the claim.

[Where A1 goes next]{.kicker}

## Pivot to the next decision

The second half of A1 turns from the past to the next real choice.

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.concept-card}
[The four questions]{.card-title}

- what is the next real design decision?
- who needs to be convinced?
- what evidence would matter?
- which pathway might help most?
:::

::: {.reflection-card}
This is where A1 stops being a post-mortem and starts pointing at the rest of the semester.
:::
::::

## Round table on YOUR evidence

::: {.spine-rail}
[Decision]{.node} [Evidence]{.node .is-current} [Variation]{.node} [Output]{.node} [Threshold]{.node} [Action]{.node}
:::

Upload one marked-up decision image (the Week 1 image, diagram, or board fragment), then we audit the evidence together. [feeds A1]{.feeds-tag}

---

## The audit (everyone)

::: {.audit-card}
[Examine the work, not the person]{.card-title}
We ask the same question of every artifact, including mine: **what does this evidence actually support, and what does it not show yet?**

Speak for 60–90 seconds. The strongest move is naming your own weakest link first.

Volunteers go first; random draw may fill the remaining examples.
:::

---

## Reconstruct your decision in four steps

**Object this week: the evidence behind your past decision.**

::: {.recall-4step}
::: {.step}
**Did** What evidence did I actually use, and for which decision?
:::
::: {.step}
**Assumed** What did I treat as evidence that was really assumption or precedent?
:::
::: {.step}
**Risk** Where was my confidence stronger than the evidence supported?
:::
::: {.step}
**Verify** What evidence would I gather before the next decision?
:::
:::

::: {.grading-note}
Post your filled four-step to Slack under your image. Posting + an honest reconstruction is the graded unit — not how you spoke.
:::

## A1 reality check

If your A1 is still vague, it is usually because:

- the original decision was too broad
- the evidence types are mixed together
- the next decision is still a theme instead of a choice
- the audience for the evidence is still unclear

::: {.reflection-card}
Vague is normal at Week 2. Naming why it is vague is the fix.
:::
